thesis: Choose a wealth-building route by whose capital and whose business are involved, accounting for control, time and responsibility.
summary: The four-box framework distinguishes bootstrapping, raising equity, investing personal capital in others, and managing pooled outside capital. Bootstrapping preserves control but can create operational and technical compromises; fundraising enables capital-intensive opportunities while introducing dilution, preferences and investor incentives. Investing generally requires surplus earned elsewhere and patience. Fund management adds sourcing, risk, reporting and regulatory responsibilities. Alex describes having participated in all four, including privately raised real-estate deals.

insights.title: Separate four routes by ownership and capital
insights.explanation: The two axes separate operating a company from allocating capital, while allowing real businesses to combine routes over time.

synthesis_method: Direct Codex extraction from complete local transcript; exact quotations verified locally
context_and_limits: The richest-person sample is selected on extreme success and does not establish typical outcomes. Biography, rankings and personal track records are unverified. In the illustrative fund waterfall, 900 minus 200 debt principal, 100 debt payments, 95 LP capital and 40 preference leaves 465 million BEFORE a proposed 50/50 split, not necessarily GP proceeds. GP contributed capital and other terms are incompletely modeled. A preferred return is a distribution priority, not guaranteed payment; leveraged losses and fees also matter. Good deals do not assure financing.
review_changes: Adds capital-structure terms, founder/investor incentive divergence, the very long feedback loop and specific limitations in the illustrative leveraged fund arithmetic.
